title: Scope before code: how I kick off freelance MVPs
excerpt: The kickoff ritual I use before writing client code: discovery, written scope, three-band estimate, deposit, and a change-request path so quick extras do not erase the plan.
metaDescription: Freelance MVP kickoff process: discovery call, written scope, estimate bands, deposit, and change requests before you write production code.
author: Ali Hamza
body:
## The expensive mistake

Starting a client MVP in a chat thread feels fast. It is not. Without a written scope, every new message can redefine the product. You either eat the cost or fight about it later.

I learned this the hard way on a dashboard build where "just like the mock" quietly grew into three roles, email alerts, and a reporting export. The mock never said that. The chat history did, after the fact. I shipped late and underpaid for the real work.

Now I kick off with paper (or Markdown) before a repo.

## Step 1: Discovery that fits one call

I keep discovery to a single focused call when I can. I ask for:

- Who the user is and what they do today without the product
- The one outcome that means version one worked
- Must-have vs later
- Logins, payments, admin needs, and data sensitivity
- Deadline and who approves changes

If the client cannot answer those, we are not ready to estimate. I would rather reschedule than invent requirements.

I also ask what must not happen. "No payment gateway in v1" or "no native app" saves weeks of polite confusion.

## Step 2: One-page scope

The scope names:

- In-scope screens and flows
- Out-of-scope items (written explicitly)
- Assumptions (APIs that exist, content the client will provide, who designs UI)
- Definition of done for the first release

I send this for written sign-off. A thumbs-up in chat is not enough. I want a reply that says the scope is accepted, or a redlined version I can merge.

When the scope is fuzzy, I shrink v1. A thin working path beats a wide unfinished surface.

## Step 3: Three-band estimate

I price lean / standard / protected bands so the client sees tradeoffs.

- **Lean** - happy path only, client provides copy and assets on time
- **Standard** - realistic buffer for auth, admin, and staging polish
- **Protected** - unclear third-party APIs, design churn, or multi-role admin

A deposit (often around 40%) starts the work. The protected band exists so "we will figure the API out later" has a price attached.

I put calendar weeks next to each band. Money without time is half a plan.

## Step 4: Change requests

After sign-off, new work goes on a change-request sheet: what changed, why, impact on timeline and price. This keeps the relationship adult when "one more button" appears.

I do not treat every idea as hostility. I treat every idea as a decision. Decisions need a record.

## What I refuse to start without

- A signed or clearly accepted scope
- Deposit cleared
- Access list (domains, repos, analytics, design files)
- A single approver on the client side

Two approvers with conflicting taste will burn your buffer faster than a hard bug.

## Tools I use

I packed this ritual into **Scopefirst**, a kickoff pack with a filled clinic example. The point is not the PDF. The point is repeating the same clear steps on every engagement so I do not reinvent the process under pressure.

## After kickoff

Only then do I open the repo: Next.js or the stack the constraint requires, staging on Vercel, and a short week-one plan. Code without scope is expensive theater.

Week one usually means: auth skeleton, one primary flow, staging URL, and a checklist of open questions. I share that early so surprises surface while they are still cheap.

## FAQ

**What if the client hates paperwork?**
Keep the scope to one page. Long contracts scare people. Vague chats bankrupt freelancers.

**What if they want to "start coding and refine"?**
I offer a paid discovery week with a written deliverable. Exploration is work. It should be paid and bounded.

**What if scope changes mid-build?**
That is normal. The change-request sheet is the product. Without it, you are guessing who owns the delay.

## Bottom line

If you are stuck mid-project without a written scope, stop coding for a day, write the one-pager, and reset expectations with the client. The repo can wait. The relationship cannot survive endless invisible expansion.

If you want help shipping a client MVP with a clear scope first, use the contact page and tell me what you are building.
